title: Workers' Comp Lawyer Cost: State Fee Caps and Approval Rules (2026)
description: How workers' comp lawyers are paid: verified attorney fee caps and approval rules for 20 states, with worked fee examples.
h1: How much does a workers' comp lawyer cost?
summary: Workers' comp lawyers for injured workers are usually paid a percentage of benefits obtained, and most states cap that fee and require approval by the comp agency or judge. Verified caps include 20% in Illinois and North Dakota, 25% in Texas, Kansas and New Jersey, Florida's sliding 20/15/10/5% scale, and Kentucky's sliding scale with an $18,000 maximum. You normally pay nothing upfront and the fee comes out of the award or settlement.
body:
How workers' comp lawyers are paid

Workers' compensation lawyers for injured workers are almost always paid a percentage of the benefits they help you obtain, and in most states that fee is limited by law and must be approved by the workers' compensation agency or judge. You generally do not pay an hourly rate or a retainer. The fee is typically taken from the benefits awarded or the settlement, and many states protect certain benefits, especially medical care, from attorney fees.

Because fees are regulated, the hourly rates in this practice are low compared with other areas: Clio's 2025 data puts the average workers' compensation lawyer rate at $180 per hour, against $349 for all lawyers [1]. That figure matters mainly for employers and insurers, who pay their defense lawyers by the hour.

Attorney fee caps by state

This table covers the states where we verified the rule on an official statute, regulation or agency page as of October 2026. Several states also limit fees on medical benefits or require a hearing for anything above the standard percentage. For states not listed, ask your state's workers' compensation agency how claimant attorney fees are set.

Claimant attorney fee rules in workers' compensation (verified October 2026)
StateFee limitNotes
Arkansas25% of indemnity (wage-loss) benefits [2]Extra capped amounts for appeals: $500 to the full commission, $1,000 to the Court of Appeals or Supreme Court (Ark. Code 11-9-715) [2]
CaliforniaNo fixed percentage; must be reasonable and approved by the WCAB [3]Fee agreements must be submitted to the appeals board within 10 days; no fee may be taken until the board approves it (Lab. Code 4906) [3]
ColoradoOver 25% of contested benefits presumed unreasonable [4]C.R.S. 8-43-403 [4]
Florida20% of first $5,000, 15% of next $5,000, 10% of the rest (first 10 years), 5% after [5]Must be approved by a judge of compensation claims; disputed medical-only claims: alternative fee up to $1,500 once per accident at up to $150/hour (F.S. 440.34) [5]
GeorgiaNot to exceed 25% [6]Board fee approval form under O.C.G.A. 34-9-108 and Board Rule 108 [6]
Idaho25% presumed reasonable without a hearing; 30% after a hearing with briefs; 15% of permanent disability paid after 10 years [7]A higher fee needs clear and convincing proof (IDAPA 17.01.01.802) [7]
Illinois20% of compensation recovered [8]Commission may allow more after a hearing; written contract on Commission forms; no fee on undisputed medical expenses (820 ILCS 305/16a) [8]
Kansas25% of compensation recovered and paid [9]Death and total or partial disability: 25% of the sum due for 415 weeks of permanent total disability (K.S.A. 44-536(a)) [9]
Kentucky20% of first $25,000, 15% of next $25,000, 10% of the rest; maximum $18,000 [10]For contracts on or after 7/14/2018 (KRS 342.320(2)(b)) [10]
MarylandNo percentage cap found; Commission approval required [11]The Commission may order refunds of excessive fees (Lab. & Empl. 9-731) [11]
Minnesota20% of the first $275,000 of compensation awarded [12]Total fees for the same injury capped at $55,000 (Minn. Stat. 176.081) [12]
Montana20% if settled without a WC judge or Supreme Court order; 25% if the case goes to hearing [13]MCA 39-71-613; ARM 24.29.3802 [13]
New JerseyUp to 25% of the judgment [14]Reasonable fee set by the judge (N.J.S.A. 34:15-64, 2025 edition) [14]
New Mexico$22,500 maximum per claim [15]NMSA 1978, 52-1-54 [15]
New YorkSchedule set by statute, e.g. 15% of increased or schedule-loss compensation [16]Fees must be approved by the Board and become a lien on the award; fees over $1,000 need a written application (WCL 24) [16]
North CarolinaNo numeric cap; Industrial Commission approval required [17]Taking unapproved fees is a Class 1 misdemeanor (G.S. 97-90) [17]
North DakotaUp to 20% of the amount awarded [18]Subject to WSI administrative-rule maximums (N.D.C.C. 65-02-08(3)) [18]
OregonRegulated by statute and Board rules [19]Example: the ORS 656.262(11)(a) fee maximum was $6,357 for orders from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026 [19]
Texas25% of each weekly income benefit, up to 25% of total income benefits [20]28 TAC 152.1(c), implementing Labor Code 408.221 [20]
West Virginia20% of benefits, computed over a 208-week period [21]W. Va. Code 23-5-16a(a) [21]

Worked examples

Florida, $30,000 in benefits secured[5]:
20% × $5,000 = $1,000
15% × $5,000 = $750
10% × $20,000 = $2,000
Total fee = $3,750, which is 12.5% of $30,000.

Kentucky, $60,000 in benefits[10]:
20% × $25,000 = $5,000
15% × $25,000 = $3,750
10% × $10,000 = $1,000
Total fee = $9,750, below the $18,000 maximum.

Illinois, $40,000 in compensation recovered[8]: 20% × $40,000 = $8,000, with no fee on undisputed medical bills.

What to check in a workers' comp fee agreement

  • The base of the percentage. Is the fee calculated on wage-loss benefits only, or on medical benefits too? Several states exclude some medical benefits.
  • Approval. In states such as California, New York, North Carolina, Maryland and Florida, a fee is not valid until the agency or judge approves it [3][16][17][11][5]. Never pay a workers' comp lawyer directly without that approval.
  • Case costs. Ask who pays for medical records, independent medical evaluations and depositions, and whether those are deducted from your share.
  • Third-party claims. If someone other than your employer caused the injury (for example, a negligent driver), a separate personal injury claim may be possible, with a separate contingency fee. See personal injury lawyer cost.
  • Social Security. If you also apply for disability benefits, that fee is set by Social Security rules, not your state; see Social Security disability lawyer cost.

Do you need a workers' comp lawyer?

Many claims are paid without a lawyer: you report the injury, the insurer accepts it and pays medical bills and wage benefits. A lawyer is more useful when the claim is denied, benefits stop, the insurer disputes the extent of your injury, you are offered a lump-sum settlement that closes future medical care, or you are being pushed back to work before your doctor clears you. Because fees are capped and approved, the cost of a consultation is usually low; ask whether the first meeting is free.

faq.q: What percentage does a workers' comp lawyer take?
faq.a: It depends on the state, and many set the limit by law. Among states we verified, Illinois caps fees at 20% of compensation, Texas at 25% of income benefits, New Jersey at 25% of the judgment, and Florida uses a sliding scale starting at 20% of the first $5,000.

faq.q: Do I pay a workers' comp lawyer up front?
faq.a: Usually not. Fees are normally taken from the benefits or settlement after the agency or judge approves them. In states such as California and North Carolina, a lawyer may not collect a fee that has not been approved.

faq.q: Does the lawyer get a share of my medical benefits?
faq.a: Often not, or only in limited ways. Illinois, for example, bars fees on undisputed medical expenses, and Florida allows only a limited alternative fee for disputed medical-only claims. Ask how your state treats medical benefits.

faq.q: Can I negotiate a lower workers' comp fee?
faq.a: Yes. Statutory caps are maximums, not required amounts, so you can ask for a lower percentage, especially if the claim is simple or the insurer has already offered benefits.
